newsitem.title: ITALY: Cuba's Castro to attend Rome food summit - sources.
newsitem.headline: Cuba's Castro to attend Rome food summit - sources.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro will make a rare visit to Europe when he attends next month's U.N. World Food Summit in Rome, diplomatic sources said on Wednesday.
"We are still waiting for the official letter (confirming his attendance), but we know there are hotel reservations for him from November 12-18," one U.N. source told Reuters.

A separate diplomatic source confirmed that the veteran Cuban leader would come to Rome after attending an Ibero-American summit, bringing together the leaders of all Latin American countries plus those of Spain and Portugal, in Chile from November 9.

The U.N. source said Cuban diplomats were organising meetings between Castro and Italian politicians as well as looking at a possible appearance by the Communist leader in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
Castro was billed to speak at the food summit on November 15, the source said.
What has not been clarified is whether Castro will meet Pope John Paul while in Rome, the sources said. The Pope is scheduled to give the opening address to the summit on November 13.
"It is my understanding that Castro wants an invitation from the Vatican, while the Vatican thinks he should ask for an audience," one of the sources said.
Castro's visit to Rome follows closely a five-day visit to Cuba by Vatican Foreign Minister Jean-Louis Tauran, who returned to Rome on Wednesday.
Relations between the Church and Cuban state were strained after the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power, although there have been recent signs of improvements.
Tauran told reporters in Havana before his return that Cuba and the Vatican had agreed to make arrangements for the Pope to visit the communist-ruled island. No date was set.
Cuba invited the Pope to visit at the end of the 1980s but arrangements were never finalised. Cuba is the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America that the Pontiff has not visited.
The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) has said about 100 heads of state and government would attend the Rome food summit.
The meeting, whose slogan is "Food for All", aims to call attention to global hunger and find ways to distribute the world's resources more evenly.
Preparations were underway this week as delegates met at the agency's headquarters to finalise language in two documents to be issued at the summit.

The so-called Working Group had hoped to reach final agreement by Wednesday evening, although certain issues were proving difficult. "You will see a lot of people have brought a change of clothes along today knowing it will be a long night," one delegate said.
Among issues causing problems is U.S. opposition to wording which would guarantee "the right of food for all".

Diplomats have said the United States is concerned that enshrining food as a "right" could lead to lawsuits demanding aid or special trade provisions and could affect political decisions regarding embargos.
